title: The Light of the Word and the Mouth of the King
english: But you say a second meaning, that all have one way. It is said concerning those having such an opinion, that of the 'believing ones, one soul and one heart' (Acts 4:32), it is not by number, but by identity. And this identity is the first state.

And we ourselves sometimes are in disagreement with ourselves, saying: 'Is this not that?' But that is not understood. Because of this it is said: 'The one who has heard is at rest.' When one is no longer carried away by many things, but knows that which the messenger announces, he is at rest, no longer disturbed. For surely that philosopher says regarding ignorance as disturbance: 'Let us not be disturbed by the parts of substances.'

Who knows the wise? And who knows the resolution of a sentence? Wisdom illuminates a man's face. He who understands the wise is rare. For it is a matter of knowing scientifically who is wise. He who thus contemplates the wise man knows who he is and his wisdom.

No one can know a shipbuilder without examining the art by which he constructs ships. And no one can know who a painter is unless he knows the art of painting. Just as it is impossible for one to know a white body without knowing what white color is, and it is impossible for one not knowing a science to know what that science is, so it is not possible to know a wise man without having known the wisdom by which he has become wise and by which he is called wise. Surely, others recognize others, and others do not recognize others.

So who knows the judgments of the sentences of the wise? He who understands these things—being able to be intelligent and being able to be discerning—is rare, [as are] parables and obscure speech, maxims of the wise and enigmas. The resolutions of enigmatic sentences are not known by chance, but by one being wise according to the wisdom by which the sentences are brought forth. Wisdom illuminates a man's face.

This says that the wisdom of man shows his face to be luminous, not the face of the body, nor the member of the flesh, but the face of the inner man, about which the wise say: 'The light of your face has been shone upon us, Lord' (Psalm 89:15). And if the light that makes wise and makes people wise and enlightened is constructed...

In your face there is light—for your word is your image, your character—the one participating in this light is enlightened and becomes illuminated. Thus Jesus says to those who drew near to him: 'Let your light shine before men' (Matt 5:16). And he says to all: 'You are the light of the world' (Matt 5:14). The apostles are not a light perceptible to the world, that is, visible to the many of men, but of the true world. Jesus did not find sin for the one reconciled to God in Christ. This, therefore, is the face of the inner man being enlightened by wisdom. And wisdom, light, word, truth, and the other notions called concerning Christ are the same.

And the shameless one will be hated before his face. 'Guard the mouth of a king and do not be hasty regarding the word of God's oath' (Ps 101:7). The shameless one, the one not having boldness from the light and wisdom that is absent, will be hated as a reproof. This exists especially for the sophists who wish to philosophize the truth. For from much shamelessness they argue against the truth. Thus they interpret things as if they do not possess nature. Therefore he is hateful, even if he sometimes escapes through craftiness and is not hated, but indeed he is hateful. And he is hateful who is worthy of being hated, even if no one hates him. For malice, even if it be any other kind, is hateful; pleasure overcomes many who love. Many are those being seduced; and it is not as if evil is not hateful.

'Guard the mouth of a king' (Ps 101:7). Guard the mouth of the king of the truth; keep his word, live and think according to his word. For the mouth has often been demonstrated to us to signify the word. He stood by the word of God, which is called his mouth of a king, and so he acts, so he thinks, so he lives. And do not be hasty regarding the word of the oath of God. And among those outside, such a thing is hateful. He who is hasty to swear provides a ground for suspicion, unless an oath is imposed upon him by the ruler in the absence of any witness and he is compelled to swear concerning this. Therefore he said: 'Do not be hasty,' meaning: do not take a voluntary course toward swearing; do not handle an unprovable faith. If it is possible for faith to be provided, do not be hasty regarding an oath.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Knowledge of Good and Evil in the Commandment
english: One who swears to his neighbor and does not break it, thus speaking truthfully so as not to violate the oath, is not to be hated. 'You shall go out from his presence; do not stand in evil speech' [1 Tim 4:16]; for he will not do whatever he wishes, as a king exercising authority? It is possible to speak excessively regarding the shameless man, saying, 'You shall go out from his presence.' Get away from the shameless man.

These things can also be applied to the devil himself and to all evil power. For things said about men as being evil or wicked could also be said about the demons and the devil. For what is said about men as being breathing animals is not applied even to the devil or to a demon.

It is also possible to say regarding the king, before whom one must behave correctly, 'You shall go out from his presence,' meaning as one being sent away from him, as we say, 'this one came from the king.' 'Do not stand in evil speech.' This means: even if it should ever happen through ignorance to say something evil, such as a harmful lie, do not stand in it, do not remain in it. Regarding the divine utterances and words, Paul writes, 'be mindful of them' [1 Tim 4:16]. Remain in the words of God, which are unsearchable and healthy.

For will he not do whatever he wishes? Will the shameless man not do what he wills? Therefore, flee from his presence. And even if it is regarding God as a king, do not suppose that because he wishes to do something, he will escape from Him if you flee, by fleeing from His knowledge. As a king exercising authority: a king possessing authority is prevented by no one, no one stands against him, but he does whatever he wishes. Therefore, take both sides.

Either regarding the true king, God—for he does what he wishes, and no one resists him; or if it is said regarding the shameless man, it again creates fear in us to flee from him. This has been said: truly the wise man is king. The Stoics indeed say that only the wise man is king, and only the priest. For if the king is the one who rules legally, but only the wise man knows this, then only this one is king. Immediately, regarding Abraham, who was an ordinary man by chance, it was said to the discerning ones, 'You are a king before God among us' [Gen 14:18]. Even if [you are] others to others, you are [a king] before God. For a king is a king...

God is among those who are. If the word is about a shameless person, he himself is like a king exercising authority over those brought under his embassy. 'Let not sin reign in your mortal body' (Rom 6:14). The one who reigned, death, from Adam to Moses, exercises authority over those under his power and his beginning. And who will say to him: 'What will you do?' The one guarding the commandment will not know an evil word. And regarding God, it is true to say that no one says to him: 'What will you do?' And regarding the shameless and impudent king. Perhaps this shameless one may be able to bear the face of the Antichrist. For indeed there in the prophecy about him of Elijah, a certain daughter rose up and thus reproved him, saying him shameless.

The one guarding the commandment will not know an evil word. See: the one knowing the good immediately knows also the evil. But to know in this way does not mean to use, but only to know. For if a commandment is given so that 'we may turn away from evil and do good,' it is necessary also to know the evil, so that we may turn away from it and choose the good. Concerning such things the apostle writes, saying: 'Test all things, hold fast to the good; abstain from every form of evil' (1 Thess 5:21). You see, how the one testing all things knows the good, and that it is to be chosen and kept, and the evil, that it is to be fled from; it is proper to be estranged from it.

If, then, the one knowing the good saw the evil and again saw it, how does he say here that the one guarding the commandment does not know an evil word? Even though the commandment is a good word. But the one knowing the good word knows also the evil word; yet he says that the one guarding the commandment does not know an evil word, that is, he does not say that he does not know, but that he does not use it, not to know it in the way: 'even Jesus did not know the sin' (John 21:22). Thus the guardian of the commandment does not know an evil word. Let the 'not knowing a word' be either an offense or not hearing the word in the way it ought to be heard. The one hearing the word as it ought, has experience of it. But the one guarding the commandment, since he has no experience of the opposite of the commandment, will not know the evil word. And the word is often said instead of the thing. Mary, having heard the word of the angel...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Knowledge of Self and the Order of the Soul
english: He says: 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word' (Luke 1:38). Thus it shall be to me, as your word flows through me. And I will not say something paradoxical. For 'in the soul' there is also a word: 'the thought which is without being either true or false, when it is already necessary to exist as such,' or to be true or to be false. A thought is called a word because it falls under the definition of knowledge; 'for a word is that which signifies time,' and it is a word in which there is to be a speaking of truth or a speaking of a lie. Since therefore such things are thoughts, we shall call them words.

This is why the divine apostle, knowing this, says 'he has heard unspoken words' (Romans 15:9). And it seems to be a contradiction, unless we take the spoken and the unspoken to mean something different from one another. They are unspoken insofar as they are spoken only in the mind, and God imparts them to the intellect. And they possess truth or falsehood, so that according to this also they are words. They are unspoken because they are not brought forth through syllables, not being able to be written or inscribed. But that which is not brought forth through syllables is unspoken. If, however, each of the things I say is spoken—for I bring it forth through articulated voice—yet the thought, which the voice does not submit, is an unspoken word. For it possesses either the truth or the lie. They are unspoken in that they do not have [the quality of being] brought forth through syllables and articulated words, but they are words in that they possess truth or falsehood.

And the heart of the wise knows the time of judgment; for in every matter there is a time and a judgment, for much knowledge of the wise is upon it. This is what he says: the mind and the heart of the wise know 'the time of judgment,' not only that which is spoken of in the Scripture. The divine words say 'the time of judgment' regarding that time, by which all stand before the judgment of God. And he calls this time 'the day of judgment.' Here, therefore, the wise man knows all time and the judgment of every matter. Having judged the things, he imposes [his judgment], and having judged the words, he brings them forth. For he knows when it is necessary to give an answer and when not, and when to oppose a word and when to let it go for the sake of the listeners. He knows the judgment of this time, so that you might not take a spoken time, such as a day or a night, but a time, to say, such as this.

Having such a state. 'Therefore the heart of the wise man knows the time of judgment,' he knows the judgment, by which it is necessary to use the times. For in every thing there is a time and a judgment. Every thing has a time and a judgment, it is manifest. Therefore, the one able to manage things in this way, as he says timely concerning them and having judged, this one is wise and performs the work of a wise man. For the knowledge of man concerning himself is much.

And human knowledge we receive in two ways, that which he knows and that which is known to him. For example, those who are knowing of themselves possess that same word, of the one knowing and of the one being known. If they are knowing of themselves and not others are knowing of them, they themselves are the knowers and the being known. 'Therefore great is the knowledge of man concerning himself,' and that which he himself knows and that which he himself is known by.

Indeed, countless things have been moved by men toward that opinion which says, 'Know thyself.' It is one, the voice is brief, but the thought is much. He who has known himself has known that he is a created being, and he has known that he has come into being for the acquisition of virtue. He has known that the soul rules in himself and the body is ruled, and again in the soul that the rational part rules, while the desiring and the spirited parts are ruled. If these things happen in reverse, it is bad. That soul, if it is ruled by the body and rules the body, is destruction to that man; and if the rational part is ruled by the spirit or by desire, this rule is lawless.

Therefore it is necessary for the wise man to know himself and to have mastery, that 'the knowledge concerning him is much,' and that which is concerning him, which he ought to know. For if he knows that 'the knowledge concerning him is much'—since he ought to know himself—having known not a little, he will not consider himself to have been perfected in life. Even if he is with all that is possible to exist here and has received knowledge, he knows that 'he knows in part' (1 Cor 13:9) and he will not stop as some already do, but he still works toward acquiring even more knowledge, even if he knows all visible things. And, as Solomon says, you might receive 'knowledge without error' of all 'things that exist,' lifting his mind upon the invisible, he knows that he possesses knowledge in many respects. For he has comprehension of the sensible things alone.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
